title: Supreme Court rejects Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for 3rd time
description:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — The Supreme Court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is underway in the midterm elections.
The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents. 
The Supreme Court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri Supreme Court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum.
fullText:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — The Supreme Court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is underway in the midterm elections.

The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.

The Supreme Court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri Supreme Court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.

"At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos," the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. "The District Court and Court of Appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri."

Republicans had hoped the new House map — which already was used in the August primaries — could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.

The new map had targeted a district held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

"I think my reelection prospects shot up significantly," a jubilant Cleaver said after the Supreme Court ruling.

A panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had ruled Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the U.S. Constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order's effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the Supreme Court.

Republican Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins described the high court's decision as "a disappointing blow to representative democracy," but added, "I appreciate the final clarity."

The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters — nearly 1 in 4 statewide — who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts. Thousands of ballots already had been mailed, and some already have been cast.

A decision from the Supreme Court is "a big sigh of relief," said Kansas City election director Shawn Kieffer. He added, "We just want it over, so we can do our job properly."

Republicans currently hold six of Missouri's eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.

The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver's 5th Congressional District far eastward into rural Republican areas.

The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri's other congressional districts.

Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state Sen. Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.

Cleaver said the court ruling affirms the people's right to use to referendum petitions against state legislative actions they don't like.

"We just received a healthy dose of encouragement that the voice of people in the United States still matters," he said.

Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican Rep. Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the 8th Circuit's ruling and the last two appeals to the Supreme Court.

Brattin denounced Friday's decision as "a travesty," calling the switching of districts after the primary "the most unprecedented form of voter disenfranchisement in American history."

At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri's congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their U.S. House districts over the past year.

Missouri's new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact. In one case, the Missouri Supreme Court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.

Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on Aug. 4 — the day the new districts were used in the primaries — to reject the petition. He asserted referendum petitions aren't allowed for congressional redistricting.

The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Sept. 3 that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The U.S. Supreme Court let that ruling stand on Sept. 8. But minutes later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 10 blocked Clark's order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri Supreme Court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark's order.

But that wasn't the end of the matter. The 8th Circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark's blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That's what led to the latest decision from the U.S. Supreme Court.

Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said the group was pressing forward with its campaign to persuade voters to permanently reject the new map in the November referendum.

"We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab," he said in a statement.

Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court and redistricting at https://apnews.com/hub/redistricting.

fullText:
The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee, the network says.

Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network, along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.

In the latest roadblock, the White House announced in a Friday night note detailing the president’s schedule that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported.

CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks. No other outlet was listed to replace CNN in the memo, according to the network. Without a designated pooler, major networks won’t be able to televise his trip.

The network’s journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported.

The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.

MS NOW also reported being blocked from the greeting ceremony. “The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López asked network host Symone Sanders Townsend Thursday night.

But CNN was allowed to cover Trump and Xi’s visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network’s coverage of Trump’s Knoxville trip.

Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them “fake news.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.

But reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.

The White House TV press pool had abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned until their access was reinstated. CBS served as the designated pooler Friday, filming Xi and Trump at the White House during the final day of his state visit.

Trump’s disdain for the mainstream press is well-documented, including his outbursts at female journalists for asking questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war. He has repeatedly targeted CNN’s Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins for “not smiling.”

But his attempt to ban several major outlets from the White House is unprecedented.

Former President Bill Clinton — who had an affair with a young staffer, Monica Lewinsky, in the 1990s that dominated the news cycle — said at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.

“And there's a reason we have a Constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

fullText:
A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections on the platform in the latest legal setback against the social media giant that has already cost it billions of dollars.

The jury found over 43 million violations of state consumer protection law and it is now up to the judge to determine how much the company would pay, with attorneys representing the state asking for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.

"The verdict marks a significant victory for New Mexico consumers and holds one of the world's largest technology companies accountable for its conduct," the New Mexico Department of Justice said in a statement.

The two-week trial in Santa Fe centered on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for Donald Trump.

Jurors sided with prosecutors, finding Facebook made deceptive statements about protecting users' data that affected New Mexico's entire population of more than two million people. The jury also found Facebook misled the public about investigations into third-party app developers that harvest user data following the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," said Alex Burgos, a spokesperson for Meta in an email.

During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook claimed the state's evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.

The trial also addressed Facebook's policies for removing harmful content. The state claimed the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent, or inaccurate, content to proliferate. Facebook denied the claims, arguing the company has adapted its policies since the state's lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.

The jury reviewed 34 statements made by the company about data protections and content policies, finding the company deceived users about its practices in almost every case.

In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn't prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a deposition played for jurors, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company had robust systems to determine whether content should be taken down. During closing arguments, Randi McGinn, an attorney representing the state, argued that Facebook profited off harmful content, which lawyers for the company denied.

"Meta's platforms are forums for free expression. We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community. This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users' information and giving them control over their data," said Burgos.

The judge will decide on penalties at a later date, but that hearing hasn't been set yet. It will be up to the state to decide where the money will go. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices in the future.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a multistate lawsuit involving child safety issues. Buried in the 130-page settlement was an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach, making New Mexico the only state to decide to pursue a case on its own. Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, saying it was not tough enough on Meta, leaving the door open for future litigation.

Also this year, New Mexico won judgments totaling $942 million from Meta in a two-phase trial about the company's safety protections for minors. The court ordered Meta to implement new safeguards, including age-verification technology and time limits on its platforms.

Schuettler reported from Phoenix.

— Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use citizenship database ahead of midterms
description:
The US Supreme Court revived on Friday an expanded immigration database that President Donald Trump's administration said aims to combat voting by noncitizens but critics contend could disenfranchise eligible voters. 
   The justices granted the Justice Department's request to block a judge's order that had stopped state officials from using Social Security ‌numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records. 
   The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from ‌Friday's order. 
   The majority said the plaintiffs' arguments likely fail because federal law expressly authorizes the Department of Homeland Security to request and receive information relating to citizenship and immigration status from other agencies, including the Social Security Administration.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court revived on Friday an expanded immigration database that President Donald Trump's administration said aims to combat voting by noncitizens but critics contend could disenfranchise eligible voters.

The justices granted the Justice Department's request to block a judge's order that had stopped state officials from using Social Security ‌numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records.

The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from ‌Friday's order.

The majority said the plaintiffs' arguments likely fail because federal law expressly authorizes the Department of Homeland Security to request and receive information relating to citizenship and immigration status from other agencies, including the Social Security Administration.

The administration's data-sharing arrangement is ​one in a series of actions boosting the federal government's involvement in voting ahead of November's midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress. The U.S. Constitution gives individual states the primary authority to run and administer elections.

The Department of Homeland Security last year redesigned a federal database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, used to verify a person's citizenship and immigration status. The revamp allowed users to search many records at a time and to conduct searches using individuals' Social Security numbers.

In a social media post on Friday, James Percival, general counsel at the Department of Homeland Security, ‌replied to a post about the court's order, saying, "Yes, you read that ⁠right. We had to file an emergency petition in the Supreme Court just so we could use government data to help states stop noncitizens from illegally voting."

Since the federal database was expanded, several Republican-led states have compared their voter lists to the database, and some voters flagged as potential noncitizens have had their ⁠registrations canceled.

Critics say such election-related actions by Republicans are driven less by concerns over election security than by an attempt to gain political advantage by narrowing the electorate, risking the disenfranchisement of eligible, often Democratic-leaning voters.

Trump has carried out hardline policies toward immigration and has made false claims of widespread voting fraud including in his 2020 election loss to Democratic former President Joe Biden.

Advocacy groups that sued to block the revised SAVE system said that the ​new ​approach has resulted in people who were wrongfully identified as noncitizens being kicked off voter rolls. They have argued ​that SAVE can be outdated, meaning immigrants who have become naturalized US citizens ‌and are thus eligible to vote are sometimes labeled as noncitizens.

The modified system's overall error rate is not publicly known. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department did not provide that information when asked.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, which represents the plaintiffs, called Friday's decision "profoundly disappointing," saying it puts Americans "at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections."

In a dissent on Friday that was joined by her two fellow liberal justices, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that "the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take."

In their Supreme Court filing, the advocacy groups cited a Travis County, Texas, election official ‌who said 25% of the system's noncitizen matches there involved people who had already proven their US citizenship, and ​news reports finding that at least 81% of the system's responses in St. Louis County, Missouri, were erroneous.

The voting rights ​group League of Women Voters and privacy rights group Electronic Privacy Information Center sued in ​September 2025 to block the Trump administration's modified system. They said that the revamp violated federal privacy and other U.S. laws.

In a June ruling blocking the revamped ‌database, US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington, D.C., said the system was ​haphazardly assembled and contained unreliable citizenship data.

"All in all, ​the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," Sooknanan wrote. "This court cannot stand idly by while that happens."

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling on September 4 declined to halt Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's request to the Supreme ​Court.

In a Supreme Court filing, Justice Department lawyers called the judge's order "indefensible," ‌arguing that it "threatens the integrity" of the midterm elections.

Texas, which intervened in the case in support of the administration, has disputed claims that the system is unreliable.

Due to separate ​litigation in Florida, the Trump administration has been able to continue using its modified SAVE system in the Republican-led states of Florida, Iowa, Indiana and Ohio.

title: Justice Jackson says Supreme Court intervenes too quickly in Trump cases
description:
WASHINGTON − Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson continued her ongoing criticism of how her colleagues are handling emergency appeals, telling an audience on Sept. 24 that requests for immediate intervention can’t become a “special avenue that certain privileged litigants can use selectively.”

She did so last year when the court allowed the administration to block $783 million in grants for health research.

“This is Calvinball jurisprudence with a twist,” Jackson wrote, referring to a made-up game in the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes. “Calvinball has only one rule: There are no fixed rules. We seem to have two: that one, and this Administration always wins.”

The rulings she referenced came on emergency requests from the administration to let a controversial policy move forward while it’s being challenged in court.

When major policies of President Donald Trump have come before the justices for a final ruling, the court permanently shut down his attempts to use emergency powers to impose tariffs and to rewrite citizenship rules.

But a majority has more often than not sided with the president on the interim decisions about Trump’s policies that are decided without a full record or oral arguments.

Jackson said the Supreme Court didn’t use to get involved as often in the early stages of the litigation. Instead, the justices “waited humbly until the facts were established and the lower courts had fully and fairly assessed the law.”

“It was only in exigent circumstances, actual emergencies, that the justices felt the need to intervene in pending cases,” she said. “I think the justices understood that very little good comes from taking an institution that is supposed to be operating outside of the political realm and routinely steering it into the fray.”

But in recent years, Jackson said, the court “has been noticeably less restrained, especially with respect to pending cases that involve controversial matters.”

In those cases, Jackson said, anyone seeking the court’s early help should have to show that something harmful is about to happen “in the real world” without intervention.

If they can do that, then the justices should issue a ruling based on which side will experience the greater harm.

“We have an appellate review process with an equitable emergency exception that can sometimes warrant the Supreme Court’s early intervention, but only when exigent circumstances require it,” she said. “I feel strongly that we should be sticking to that history and tradition.”

A federal appeals court has rebuffed a Trump administration effort to dictate how homeless service organizations in Los Angeles can seek millions of dollars in funding from the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The ruling released Thursday also frees up federal funding that already had been approved but not distributed to homeless service organizations in Los Angeles.

At issue was whether the Los Angles Homeless Services Authority could submit an application on behalf of dozens of organizations seeking $239 million in federal funds.

In a 2-1 decision posted Thursday, the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a district court ruling that restored LAHSA as the applicant for the organizations seeking federal funds.

HUD suspended LAHSA in June, citing a record of mismanagement, and said organizations should apply directly to the government for the 2026-27 funding cycle. The initial application deadline was the end of August.

LAHSA sued to block the move. District Court Judge David O. Carter issued a preliminary injunction finding that HUD acted arbitrarily and capriciously and ordered it to restore LAHSA's authority. He set a trial date in February.

HUD then appealed, seeking a stay.

In its bluntly worded decision, the appellate panel denied the department's request, finding that HUD "chose to suspend LAHSA at a time when it would leave the Los Angeles region particularly vulnerable" with ill effects on "vulnerable populations, critical programs and ongoing services."

"It is likely that its plan is unworkable and, at this late stage, extremely difficult if not virtually impossible to implement," the decision said.

Stephanie Graves, chair of the LAHSA Commission, applauded the court's ruling. "For the thousands of people experiencing homelessness or working to rebuild their lives, the systems and funding that connect them to housing and services cannot simply stop," Graves said in a statement. "Today's decision allows that work to continue while the larger issues are resolved."

The new deadline to apply for HUD funding is Oct. 14, and LAHSA's Interim Chief Executive Officer Gita O'Neill said the agency is "moving at full speed" to meet that deadline.

In addition to leaving LAHSA as the applicant for this funding cycle, the order also requires HUD to release funds from last year's grants that had been approved but not formally released by the department, forcing about a dozen Los Angeles organizations to operate for months without reimbursement.

"Today's 9th Circuit decision is welcome news for the survivors of domestic violence and their children who depend on Jewish Family Service LA's Hope Transitional Shelter," the group said in a statement. "But a court ruling alone does not solve our funding crisis."

Since April 1, the shelter has operated without $300,000 in promised government funding, covering half its budget.

"HUD's appeal is still underway, and until these funds actually reach providers, the situation at our Hope Transitional Shelter remains critical," the statement said.

The order also restored LAHSA's other core functions — operating the homeless database and the housing matching system and conducting the annual homeless count. But the reprieve is only temporary. As directed in Carter's ruling, the board of the federally mandated committee that has perennially selected LAHSA for those functions issued a request for proposals from other applicants.

Los Angeles County, which last year diverted its more than $300 million in homeless funds from LAHSA to the new Department of Homeless Services and Housing, applied to take over all those functions.

Thursday's decision was signed by justices Jacqueline H. Nguyen, an Obama appointee and Roopali H. Desai, a Biden appointee. Trump appointee Ryan D. Nelso dissented.

fullText:
UK watchdog fined video app in 2023 for failing to enforce minimum age limit and remove underage users

TikTok will pay a £12.7m fine to the UK’s data watchdog after dropping an appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.

The video app was punished by the Information Commissioner’s Office in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform, and failing to remove underage users.

When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.

TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020, the ICO said. TikTok also failed to provide users with information about how their data was being collected and used, and neglected to obtain parental consent.

Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”

Chinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”.

TikTok, which has more than 30m users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and how it serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.

At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.

“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.

Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.

The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has said “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. In Australia, which introduced a social media ban for under-16s last December, the eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.

fullText:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., issued a temporary restraining order on Thursday, ordering the White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters who had been banned by President Trump.

In his 8-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, ordered the White House to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" access to the news outlets for a period of 14 days, saying their lawsuit against the president was likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process.

But hours after the ruling was issued, some reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were still denied access to the White House grounds, and the outlets requested an immediate hearing.

"This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in a court filing early Thursday. I

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to respond to the accusations of non-compliance by midday on Thursday. It was not immediately clear when a hearing might take place.

Trump announced the ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 18, saying the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration.

The three news organizations filed a lawsuit in federal court Monday, alleging that Trump had violated their First Amendment rights by retaliating against them for coverage he didn't like.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint stated. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argued that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing stated.

Dozens of media organizations signed an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

The Trump administration filed a response to the suit on Tuesday, arguing that "access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."

It said that Trump concluded that the three news outlets violated "the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."

Trump had previously indicated that he would appeal any ruling against him.

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

In response to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday, including his trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

Speaking with reporters after arriving at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump appeared to take issue with the presence of CNN's Kaitlan Collins, saying he was "surprised" to see the journalist.

"You should not be here covering me," Trump said. "You said you weren't going to be covering me."

In a post on X, Collins said she was credentialed by the United Nations to cover the General Assembly.

CNN is scheduled to serve as the television pool Chinese President President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Thursday night.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the ban in an appearance on NBC's Today show earlier Tuesday.

"We're not closing CNN," Rubio said. "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

During his first term in office, Trump continued the Oval Office's adversarial relationship with the media, referring to the press as "fake news" and the "enemy of the people." It has escalated in his second.

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and Kelly, the D.C. federal judge, ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A different federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In December, the Pentagon announced new restraints on journalists, who were asked to sign a pledge affirming that they would not gather unauthorized information for publication. New organizations refused to sign the pledge, and temporarily lost their credentials. The New York Times filed suit, and in March, a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon restrictions were unconstitutional. The Pentagon restored press credentials to the journalists who refused to sign the pledge, while imposing a new rule that they can only enter the Pentagon with an escort. The Times again filed suit and the case is ongoing.

The White House has also made attempts to circumvent traditional broadcast television models. On Monday night, it launched a YouTube stream branded "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station" that the White House said would showcase "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."

Since its launch, Trump TV has featured a rotating stream of Trump's speeches, Oval Office gatherings and other White House events from throughout the president's second term.

The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

In March, the White House launched an official app that is now the No. 2 most popular news app in the App Store. "The American people are not waiting on those cameras," the White House said in a press release touting the app's ranking. "They are going straight to the Presidency."

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

He opened by reminding both sides that he's required to apply case precedent.

The rulings in two prior cases over press access — including one that went to the U.S. Supreme Court — made clear that journalists were entitled to an opportunity to be heard before they have their press passes revoked.

Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik has argued that the rulings in the earlier cases were wrong.

"Maybe they were, maybe they weren't, but currently as a district judge I have to apply them," Kelly said.

Arguments began with Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, calling the ban an "unprecedented, unreasonable punishment" and saying there was "not a semblance of due process."

Velchik told the court that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right."

"The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security," he added.

The administration has doubled down on its contention that it has the right to decide who can set foot in the White House.

In filing late Tuesday, administration lawyers argued that the ban does not violate the First Amendment, which guarantees the right to a free press. It contended that the outlets, in their reporting, violated "standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues and publishing sensitive or classified information."

The administration went on to detail letters that were sent to each outlet that identified "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods."

The "reporting incidents" cited in the filing included: CNN reporting on "'top-secret' construction details related to the East Wing bunker"; MS NOW reporting "on an alleged leak investigation"; and Politico publishing "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements."

Further examples were given in individual letters. Politico's letter detailed six incidents of reporting, including in June citing a "senior administration official … granted anonymity" predicting whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran.

That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House itself. Several other outlets also reported the official's remarks.

Trump began to emphasize the national security argument Tuesday, when he said negative coverage was dangerous for the country.

"I think we have a right to clean out fake news," he told reporters at the United Nations, defending the ban, which was suddenly announced Friday. The next day, journalists for the three outlets arrived at work to find their entry badges disabled.

The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The five-network U.S. network press pool — a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, and to which CNN belongs — decided to suspend coverage of Trump events until further notice. The Associated Press joined a group of organizations that refrained from publishing photos of the president Monday. On Wednesday, the network pool was again missing from a daily White House press schedule.

The ban and subsequent lawsuit are part of a long-running conflict between the president — especially in his second term — and media outlets he finds unfavorable. Trump has responded in the courtroom, or with regulatory action. He's also lashed out at individual reporters in personal terms.

An amicus brief was filed by other news groups Wednesday, urging the court to immediately restore the three outlets' White House access.

The brief — filed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents' Association and 49 media outlets and industry groups, including The Associated Press, The New York Times and Reuters — says "the targeted expulsion of news media from White House grounds injures the public interest" and that "unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant."

The proceedings are historic, said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University.

"No president has taken this explicit of a step" to ban entire news outlets because he doesn't like their reporting, she said. "There have been various presidents throughout history who have grumbled about the press or threatened to take more major steps, but really there was nothing at this level before Trump."

Noveck reported from New York. Associated Press journalist Laurie Kellman contributed from London.

fullText:
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

The ruling from the US 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is the latest twist in a whiplash legal wrangling over the map of the state’s eight congressional districts, injecting another round of uncertainty, as it does not take effect immediately but rather sets up another round of appeals.

The Missouri Supreme Court previously said the 7-1 Republican-leaning map adopted by the legislature last year could not be used because of a referendum challenge brought against it under the state constitution. Instead, the court ordered election officials to use an older, 6-2 redistricting plan even though the 2025 plan had been used in the state’s primary. The US Supreme Court declined to reverse that ruling, and it then paused a federal judge’s ruling that sought to revive the 7-1 map.

The new ruling from the 8th Circuit said requiring voters to cast general election ballots on the older plan violates the US Constitution.

It relied on estimates put forward by a conservative group in the case to conclude “that more than 1.4 million Missourians could not vote for the congressional district nominees who will appear on their November 2026 general election ballot, and more than a quarter-million Missourians who voted in the August 2026 primary election cast a vote for a congressional district candidate who now cannot represent them.”

Missouri’s new map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state.

The group that launched the referendum campaign against the GOP-leaning map noted in a statement reacting to the new ruling that “Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted.”

“Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect,” the statement from People Not Politicians said. “Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections.”

This story has been updated to correctly reflect the number of congressional districts in Missouri.

CNN’s Fredreka Schouten and John Fritze contributed to this report.

fullText:
Sept 21 (Reuters) - A California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination at its flagship assembly plant is set to go to trial on Monday, one of a ‌series of similar lawsuits being faced by the electric vehicle maker.

Lawyers for Tesla and the California ‌Civil Rights Department will square off in Oakland before state Superior Court Judge Peter Borkon, who has scheduled the trial to run until October ​30.

In the lawsuit filed in 2022, the California Civil Rights Department claims Black workers at Tesla's Fremont, California plant were subjected to pervasive harassment by other employees, including racial slurs and graffiti, and Tesla failed to prevent or stop it. Tesla is also accused of paying Black workers less than others and depriving them of opportunities for promotions.

Tesla and ‌its lawyers did not respond to requests ⁠for comment. The company has denied wrongdoing and said that it does not tolerate discrimination and has fired workers found to have engaged in misconduct.

The California Civil Rights Department's director, ⁠Kevin Kish, in a statement said the agency looked forward to holding Tesla accountable.

Tesla's high profile and the thousands of workers involved in the case make it among the most significant involving employment discrimination claims against a major US company to ​go ​to trial in recent years.

Borkon has scheduled ​a bench trial, meaning that he and not ‌a jury will decide whether Tesla is liable for violations of California civil rights laws.

Unlike federal law, the California law barring workplace discrimination does not cap the damages a court can award to affected workers, and Tesla could be on the hook for many millions of dollars if it loses the case.

Tesla has for the last decade been dogged by claims that it fostered a climate at the Fremont plant and other facilities that was extremely ‌hostile to Black workers. The company is also facing a lawsuit ​from the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleging racial harassment, and ​dozens of lawsuits by individual workers making similar ​claims.

The claims in the Civil Rights Department's lawsuit are broader and include allegations that the ‌Fremont plant was racially segregated, with Black workers ​assigned to the lowest-paying and ​least desirable jobs.

Borkon ruled in a separate lawsuit last year that more than 6,000 Black workers could not sue Tesla as a class, reversing an earlier decision and handing a major victory to the company.

title: What is Yankees’ Aaron Judge facing? Surgeon weighs in on possible return, calf re-injury risk
description: A sports surgeon details when Yankees captain Aaron Judge might be able to return from a calf strain.
fullText:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.

The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.

Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.

At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.

The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.

1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.

2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.

3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.

How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?

As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.

"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''

Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."

What can we unpack from what little we know?

NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).

"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."

Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.

"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."

Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.

If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.

"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."

Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.

"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."

The location of his calf strain is problematic.

"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."

If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.

"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."

That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.

Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon

Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:

"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.

"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."

fullText:
A fundraiser for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who favored convicting Lindsay Clancy in her closely watched Massachusetts murder trial, has passed $300,000 on crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo.

The 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of her children—Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan—at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She pleaded not guilty.

Her defense attorney argued that postpartum psychosis had left her not criminally responsible for their deaths. The 12 jurors deliberated for seven days but failed to reach a unanimous verdict, leading Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.

"I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said in a statement previously provided to Newsweek via his lawyer. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

In a statement on Friday on X, GiveSendGo co-founder Jacob Wells said he had spoken with Desronvil and his attorney Edward Paltzik.

“The Lone Juror is being added to the campaign as the recipient. His identity has been verified,” Wells wrote. “Thank you all for your generosity to this campaign.”

In a written statement on X, Paltzik thanked Wells and the fundraiser’s organizers for ensuring that all proceeds would go directly to his client to help pay for necessities after what he described as “death threats, doxxing and harassment.”

He wrote that “Stand With the Juror” would continue as the official and authorized fundraising page, with further updates to be posted there. Paltzik also thanked Wells for his leadership of the fundraising platform and acknowledged others who helped establish and support the campaign.

As of early Saturday, the fundraiser had raised a little over $330,000 of a stated goal of $350,000.

Newsweek reached out to Clancy’s attorney for comment via email on Saturday.

Desronvil, 48, from Massachusetts was the only juror who favored finding Clancy criminally responsible at her murder trial.

His attorney described him in a statement on social media on Thursday as an “American Hero and Champion of Justice [who] loves the United States of America as the greatest country in the world.”

Paltzik added Desronvil was “presently safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England.”

Newsweek previously reported that court records showed Desronvil faced a criminal charge in 2021 for allegedly assaulting his then-wife to which he pleaded not guilty, and the charges were later dismissed, meaning he was not convicted.

Following the mistrial, the case remains unresolved and the murder charges against her are still pending.

The next confirmed court proceeding is a September 29 status hearing in Plymouth Superior Court before Sullivan. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, has filed a renewed motion asking the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty. He argued that the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence to establish criminal responsibility for the killings beyond a reasonable doubt.

Reddington has also said he intends to argue that another prosecution should be barred on double-jeopardy grounds, challenging whether there was sufficient necessity to declare the mistrial.

fullText:
WASHINGTON – If recent history is the judge, President Donald Trump faces an uncertain legal landscape after his latest attempt to ban certain media outlets from covering him at the White House.

Trump announced in a Sept. 18 social media post that he is banning reporters from three major media outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and Politico – from the White House because he views their coverage as "FAKE NEWS."

Trump later said there wasn't a specific incident or story that prompted him to initiate the ban, which would not preclue the outlets from reporting on the president.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," he said.

It's not the first time the Trump administration has taken such action against the press.

During his first term, the Trump White House in 2018 pulled the press credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, complaining that he refused to yield the microphone at a press conference. However, a federal judge appointed by Trump later forced the White House to restore the press pass, saying Acosta hadn't been given a proper chance to defend himself.

And in early 2025, the White House blocked the Associated Press from the Oval Office, The White House East Room, and the press pool that sometimes travels with the president. The White House was upset because the AP declined to change its style for describing the gulf bordering the U.S. and Mexico from the "Gulf of Mexico" to the "Gulf of America." Trump had ordered the name change on official maps.

In the AP's case, one federal trial judge appointed by Trump temporarily blocked the ban. But two appeals court judges - also appointed by Trump - on the three-judge panel reversed that decision in a 2-1 ruling. The case is still being litigated.

The past controversial decisions make for an uncertain legal landscape if the latest media outlets decide to take the White House to court for the most recent ban.

A spokesperson for CNN told USA TODAY in a statement that the ban Trump proposes would be an "illegal assault" on the press. The network said it plans to continue its coverage.

"CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting," the statement said. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government."

Politico, in a statement, said the publication "will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones" and "will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."

Representatives of MS NOW declined to comment.

Trump dismissed concerns about violating the Constitution, telling reporters that the move is justified "because they’re fake news."

The president suggested he wanted to make a point, regardless of whether the ban withstands a court challenge.

"We'll see," Trump said when asked what makes him think his ban will be upheld in court. "I think it’s good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn’t . . . depends on the judge you get, to be honest with you. I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump added. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my, into the people’s house.”

Trump had few details on what the ban means in practical terms ‒ whether it's the revocation of press badges, removal from the White House pool, or blocking reporters from the targeted outlets from entering the White House campus.

“A very simple ban," Trump said. "I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can.”

The president bristled when a reporter asked whether he's trying to intimidate the media from doing its job. "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press," the president said.

The AP initially had success in its lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's ban. Washington, D.C. federal trial Judge Trevor McFadden, who was appointed by Trump, ruled the ban probably violated the First Amendment's free speech protections and issued a temporary order blocking it.

"(U)nder the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists - be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere - it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints," McFadden wrote.

However, in a 2-1 decision governed by two other Trump appointees, Judges Neomi Rao and Gregory G. Katsas, an appeals court panel largely struck down McFadden's order. It said blocking the White House from restricting specific reporters' ability to join other reporters in the Oval Office or the press pool interferes with the president's authority.

"While the AP has alleged financial loss from being denied access to the Oval Office, that harm does not, inour view, justify an intrusion on presidential prerogatives during this litigation," Rao wrote, in an opinion joined by Katsas.

Judge Cornelia T.L. Pillard, an appointee of President Barack Obama, dissented, writing that her colleages' view "cannot be squared with . . . any sensible understanding of the role of a free press in our constitutional democracy."

Trump's latest targeted reporter ban appears to go further than the ban on the AP, barring reporters "from the White House," according to his social media post.

That may not hold muster even with the judges who largely ruled with the Trump administration before. Those judges did overturn an attempt by the White House to block the AP from accessing the White House's East Room, noting it is "a much larger space that can accommodate more members of the press." And those judges specifically noted the ban on the AP didn't block it from entering White House press facilities such as the main briefing room.

The AP's case is still under litigation.

Clay Calvert, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, called the bans “thoroughly unsurprising,” particularly as Trump faces low approval ratings heading into the midterms. The institute is a Washington-based public policy think tank.

The news media is an “easy target” for Trump, Calvert said, and implementing the ban is likely to appeal to his political base that overwhelmingly distrusts mass media.

Though it echoes Trump’s earlier ban on the Associated Press, Calvert described that as a “much more precise target” centered on a single decision – the news outlet refusing to adopt “Gulf of America” after Trump renamed the body of water widely known as the “Gulf of Mexico.” The ban was also limited to certain spaces, including Air Force One and the Oval Office.

It's not immediately clear whether CNN, MS NOW and Politico would face similar restrictions or be barred from the White House entirely.

Barring journalists from the White House or other spaces where the government operates can make it “really difficult” to get information to report to the wider public, ACLU senior policy counsel Jenna Leventoff told USA TODAY.

A federal judge blocked a press policy the Pentagon implemented in 2025 that said journalists who "solicit" information not approved for public release could lose access to the building. The Pentagon then imposed an interim press policy that required journalists to be escorted through the premises at all times, which was also struck down.

But the potential to get involved in a costly and time-consuming legal fight with the Trump administration may make some news outlets “think twice” about their reporting, Leventoff said.

“In that respect, it doesn’t matter if he wins in court or not, because he’s still chilling the media from saying things he dislikes,” she said.

National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in the organization’s news release on the matter that Trump “weakens one of the nation’s strongest checks on those who hold power” by blocking access to his administration.

He said the latest ban would be an “unprecedented assault on press freedom” if implemented and underscored journalists’ role in informing the American public.

“A government confident in its actions should never fear independent scrutiny,” he said.

title: Cal won't judge its next opponent by its 87-3 loss. Its own offense has work to do
description: Tosh Lupoi's Bears hope to build a winning streak and overwhelm visiting Wagner this weekend, while Stanford heads to Duke and San Jose State has its home opener.
fullText:
While Cal football is heavily favored against a Wagner team that lost 87-3 the previous week, the Bears are not taking their FCS opponents lightly.

"I've learned in 20 years of coaching, the last thing you're doing is allowing the last performance to be the judgment of a team," head coach Tosh Lupoi said Tuesday. Wagner is "top 20 in the FCS in bringing pressure and top 20 in creating TFLs; that's problematic. That's what I'm looking at, and just like us, it's a clean slate moving forward."

And it's not like Cal can afford to take the outcome for granted, given their offensive inconsistencies. Through two games, the Bears offense ranks 86th in the country in points per game (25.3) and 89th in yards per game (357.6). In their 17 possessions since the 8:28 mark in the third quarter of Cal's 45-24 season opener loss to UCLA, the Bears have found the end zone just twice. If not for defensive back Kingston Lopa's fourth-quarter pick-six to take the decisive 21-18 lead, the Bears might have come up short against Syracuse.

It's a problem that falls on offensive coordinator Jordan Somerville, who expressed belief that the offense is capable of much more than what they have shown thus far.

"We still believe that there's no doubt about it; we got an explosive unit," the first-year offensive coordinator said Tuesday. "Fundamentals go back to the basics. Trust our training."

It's not a question of talent. With a quarterback as gifted as Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele, surrounded by touted skill position players from the transfer portal, the Bears have the pieces of a potent offense. But it's on Somerville to put it together. And while it's early and there are sure to be some growing pains with a first-time play caller and a sophomore quarterback, Cal invested a lot of money in its offense. At some point this season, the bill has to come due.

But for Lupoi, it's less about the play-calling and more about the execution.

"Jordan Somerville is doing an awesome job. He's open-minded to seeing who we are, how we can utilize our personnel best," Lupoi said. "And when you dive into that film, within the last two weeks, we've had seven balls that … it hits the hands, and it's dropped. We've got to do that at a better level. We can't just be saying, 'Catch the ball,' is a poor coaching point."

Luckily for Cal, Wagner is the perfect kind of opponent to iron out the kinks in the offense. At least, in theory. The Bears will kick off against the Seahawks in Memorial Stadium at 12:30pm PST.

After a thorough 45-6 thrashing by the powerhouse Miami Hurricanes two weeks ago, Stanford heads across the country to Duke with a focus on tightening up their schemes.

"When you look at our first two games, there were times when we lost focus. We lost focus on what our job was. And that starts with me," coach Tavita Pritchard told reporters Wednesday, explaining that the team spent the past two weeks drilling the little things like technique and foot placement.

"I resist the phrase 'get back to the basics,' because I think you should never leave the basics. It's about really making sure the fundamentals of what we do within our systems - offense, defense, and special teams - that we are very detailed in our approach to those things."

The details will have to be up to par as the Cardinal face an electric Blue Devils offense. Sophomore running back Nate Sheppard is second in the country with 374 rushing yards through two games this season. Paired with quarterback Walker Eget, who last season with San Jose State burned the Cardinal defense for 473 yards and three touchdowns, Duke's offense will look to generate big plays against a Stanford defense prone to giving up large gains.

For their own offense, Stanford will turn to quarterback Davis Warren to keep pace with the Blue Devils, which starts by limiting turnovers.

"He's going to have to be really on it this week," Pritchard said. "This defense has created a lot of turnovers, and they won our conference championship game because they had a defense that is opportunistic."

It's a tricky tightrope act - limiting turnovers while staying aggressive against Duke's ball-hawking defense, Pritchard explained, but he trusts Warren to deliver.

"When the opportunities present themselves, he's done a good job of taking those plays where they exist," Pritchard said. "He has to keep living in that space in that balance of protecting the ball but playing with an attacking mindset."

Stanford kicks off against Duke at the Wallace Wade Stadium at 1 p.m. PST, the teams' first meeting since 2012. The Cardinal are 3-1 all-time versus the Blue Devils.

While conference realignment has torn apart some historic rivalries, San Jose State vs. Fresno State remains testy as the two programs meet for the first time since the Bulldogs left the Mountain West for the Pac-12 this past year.

Which is why Spartans head coach Ken Niumatalolo is taking a measured approach.

"We recognize this is our big rivalry game, and we got to do the best we can to get ready. But all you can worry about is between the white lines," Niumatalolo told reporters Thursday, more focused on San Jose State's habit of slow starts the past couple of games. "Obviously it's big for our school and our fans, but if we don't play well, it doesn't matter."

The Spartans will lean on running back Jabari Bates, who's third in the country with 319 rushing yards, as well as quarterback Luke Weaver, who has thrown for 788 yards and three TDs through three games this season.

Despite Niumatalolo downplaying the emotion around this game, he still believes it is important for San Jose State as they try to build a winning streak.

"Going into conference play, we want to continue that positive trend that we're going in," Niumatalolo said. "I know it's going to be hard, but I think this will be monumental for us for the rest of the season. This is a huge game."

San Jose State faces Fresno State in their home opener at 8 p.m. PST.

Kenzo Fukuda is a freelance journalist born and raised in San Francisco. He has covered the Giants, Warriors and Valkyries since 2025, and he previously covered Cal football and women's basketball from 2022-24. You can follow him on X at @kenzofuku

There's more to San Francisco with the Chronicle.

title: Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial says he 'didn't have any doubts'
description:
He was the sole holdout on a 12-person jury who otherwise voted to acquit Lindsay Clancy of murdering her three children — frustrating the defense and causing a mistrial.
After seven days of deliberations, and with specific instructions from Judge William Sullivan to follow the letter of the law on reasonable doubt, the jury said it still had one holdout who refused to budge. A mistrial was declared on Sept. 4.
